extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy / economists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the principles determining wages, profits, and interest as presented in a classical political-economy text (relations among price of provisions, demand for labour, stock, competition, and legal/institutional factors). Useful for analyzing historical and theoretical criteria about labour and capital markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of price of provisions on labour supply and wages
rubrics_metrics.description: In years of plenty, servants frequently leave their masters, and trust their subsistence to what they can make by their own industry... Cheap years tend to increase the proportion of independent workmen to journeymen and servants of all kinds, and dear years to diminish it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheap seasons increase the fund for maintenance of servants and encourage masters (especially farmers) to employ more servants; many leave service to work independently, increasing demand for labour and sometimes raising wages in cheap years. In scarcity, people return to service, increasing labour supply and often lowering wages. Examples: observations from various manufactures and localities; many goods made in cheap years may not appear in public registers because they are for family use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money price of labour determined by demand for labour and price of necessaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The money price of labour is necessarily regulated by two circumstances; the demand for labour, and the price of the necessaries and conveniencies of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand for labour (increasing, stationary, declining) determines the quantities of necessaries that must be given; the money price of labour is determined by what is requisite for purchasing this quantity. Thus wages reflect both labour demand and cost of living; when demand is constant, higher price of provisions would raise money wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposing forces explain why wages don't always move with provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the variations in the price of labour not only do not always correspond with those in the price of provisions, but are frequently quite opposite... In the ordinary variations of the prices of provisions, those two opposite causes seem to counterbalance one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two opposing effects—(a) price of provisions tends to raise wages when provisions are dear, and (b) demand for labour tends to rise in cheap years and fall in dear years—can offset each other, making wages steadier than provisions. Sudden abundant years raise demand and may raise both real and money wages; sudden scarcity does the opposite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase of stock raises wages and tends to lower profits
rubrics_metrics.description: The increase of stock, which raises wages, tends to lower profit. When the stocks of many rich merchants are turned into the same trade, their mutual competition naturally tends to lower its profit...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As capital (stock) accumulates, employers compete for labour (raising wages) and competition among employers reduces profit rates. The effect operates across trades when stock increases generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest rate as an indicator of ordinary profits of stock
rubrics_metrics.description: Some notion may be formed of [profits of stock] from the interest of money. It may be laid down as a maxim, that wherever a great deal can be made by the use of money, a great deal will commonly be given for the use of it; and that, wherever little can be made by it, less will commonly be given for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market rate of interest tends to vary with ordinary profits: as market interest rises or falls, ordinary profits generally do likewise. Historical statutory interest rates followed, rather than led, market rates (examples given through English history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits of stock are more fluctuating and harder to average than wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Profit is so very fluctuating, that the person who carries on a particular trade, cannot always tell you himself what is the average of his annual profit... It varies, therefore, not only from year to year, but from day to day, and almost from hour to hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profits are affected by price variations of commodities, fortunes of rivals and customers, and many accidents in transport and storage—hence difficulty in ascertaining average profits across trades or through history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition among many large stocks reduces profits
rubrics_metrics.description: When the stocks of many rich merchants are turned into the same trade, their mutual competition naturally tends to lower its profit...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An increase of capital applied to a trade increases competition among capitalists and reduces ordinary profit in that trade (applies both to individuals and to a society when stock increases in many trades).

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban vs rural differences: larger stock and higher wages in towns lower profits
rubrics_metrics.description: It generally requires a greater stock to carry on any sort of trade in a great town than in a country village... The great stocks employed in every branch of trade, and the number of rich competitors, generally reduce the rate of profit in the former below what it is in the latter. But the wages of labour are generally higher in a great town than in a country village.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In thriving towns capitalists compete for labour (raising wages) and for business (lowering profit); in remote country places, insufficient stock implies lower wages and higher profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory regulation of interest follows market rate; prohibitions ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: All these different statutory regulations seem to have been made with great propriety. They seem to have followed, and not to have gone before, the market rate of interest... When the law prohibits interest altogether, it does not prevent it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical English statutes adjusted legal rates to prevailing market conditions. Prohibitions or caps on interest do not stop lending; they may increase evasion and usury. Examples: statutes from Henry VIII through Queen Anne; Montesquieu's account of Mahometan nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: New colonies: understocking leads to high wages, high profits, and high interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A new colony must always, for some time, be more understocked in proportion to the extent of its territory, and more underpeopled in proportion to the extent of its stock... Such land, too, is frequently purchased at a price below the value even of its natural produce. Stock employed in the purchase and improvement of such lands, must yield a very large profit, and, consequently, afford to pay a very large interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In new settlements abundant fertile land and scarce capital/labour produce high returns to capital and high wages; as colony fills and less fertile land must be cultivated, profits and interest fall (historical observation in North American and West Indian colonies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminution of capital stock raises profits and interest and lowers wages
rubrics_metrics.description: The diminution of the capital stock of the society, or of the funds destined for the maintenance of industry, however, as it lowers the wages of labour, so it raises the profits of stock, and consequently the interest of money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With less capital, the cost of producing goods falls for owners (lower labour costs) and less competition among capitalists raises profit margins, enabling higher interest. Example: Bengal and other ruined countries where wages very low and profits/usury very high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowest ordinary rate of profit must exceed expected losses; interest limited by clear profit
rubrics_metrics.description: The lowest ordinary rate of profit must always be something more than what is sufficient to compensate the occasional losses to which every employment of stock is exposed... The interest which the borrower can afford to pay is in proportion to the clear profit only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gross profit often includes retained sums for extraordinary losses; only 'clear' profit can sustain interest payments. Interest rates must be high enough to cover expected occasional losses of lending; otherwise lending would only be charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fully stocked and fully peopled country yields very low wages and profits
rubrics_metrics.description: In a country which had acquired that full complement of riches... both the wages of labour and the profits of stock would probably be very low... In a country fully stocked in proportion to all the business it had to transact... the ordinary profit as low as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When land, stock, and population are all near their equilibrium (no more gains from additional stock or people), competition reduces ordinary profits and wages to bare subsistence/small returns; hypothetical/state examples: China & Holland discussed as near different extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional insecurity/defective law raises interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A defect in the law may sometimes raise the rate of interest considerably above what the condition of the country... would require. When the law does not enforce the performance of contracts, it puts all borrowers nearly upon the same footing with bankrupts...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak contract enforcement increases lender risk; lenders charge higher interest to compensate. Historical example: barbarous nations after Roman fall; Montesquieu on Mahometan nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition or moral proscription of interest does not eliminate usury; often increases it
rubrics_metrics.description: In the reign of Edward VI. religious zeal prohibited all interest. This prohibition, however, like all others of the same kind, is said to have produced no effect, and probably rather increased than diminished the evil of usury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bans on interest lead to evasion, underground lending at higher rates. Examples include historical English prohibitions and other nations where interest persists despite prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between interest and clear profit varies with ordinary profit levels
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion which the usual market rate of interest ought to bear to the ordinary rate of clear profit, necessarily varies as profit rises or falls... In a country where the ordinary rate of clear profit is eight or ten per cent. it may be reasonable that one half of it should go to interest...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fraction of clear profit allocable to interest depends on overall profit levels; when ordinary profits are low, less can be paid as interest; when high, more may be afforded. Practical example: merchants' notion of 'double interest' as a reasonable return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquisition of new territory or trade can temporarily raise profits and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The acquisition of new territory, or of new branches of trade, may sometimes raise the profits of stock, and with them the interest of money... The stock of the country, not being sufficient for the whole accession of business... is applied to those particular branches only which afford the greatest profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New profitable opportunities draw capital away from older trades, reducing competition there and raising prices and profits in those older trades; overall effect raises market interest for a time (example: post-war accession of North American and West Indian trade).

rubrics_metrics.name: High profits raise prices more than high wages (compound vs arithmetic effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: In raising the price of commodities, the rise of wages operates in the same manner as simple interest does in the accumulation of debt. The rise of profit operates like compound interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wage increases add arithmetically at each stage of manufacture (sum of added wages), while profit increases add multiplicatively (each employer adds a percentage on top of already increased values), so high profits have a larger cumulative effect on final prices than equivalent increases in wages. Illustrated with linen manufacture and the geometric accumulation of profit across production stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaints about high wages ignore the larger price effect of high profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Our merchants and master manufacturers complain much of the bad effects of high wages in raising the price, and thereby lessening the sale of their goods... They say nothing concerning the bad effects of high profits; they are silent with regard to the pernicious effects of their own gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers tend to blame wages for higher prices while overlooking how profits (their own) multiply through production and raise prices more significantly; rhetorical and analytical caution about attributing price rises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages and disadvantages of different employments tend toward equality
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole of the advantages and disadvantages of the different employments of labour and stock, must, in the same neighbourhood, be either perfectly equal, or continually tending to equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one employment is evidently more advantageous, people will enter it until its advantages fall back to the level of others; conversely, people will leave less advantageous employments—mechanism of mobility equalizing returns across local employments.
